clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, typically congenital and non-progressive (or very slowly progressive) cerebellar ataxia caused by heterozygous ITPR1 variants.
Presents in infancy with hypotonia and delayed motor milestones, later evolving into gait ataxia, dysarthria and titubation.
Nystagmus and other oculomotor abnormalities and intention tremor are frequent; learning difficulties or cognitive impairment occur in a subset.
Many cases arise de novo, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis.
ITPR1 is allelic with SCA15 (usually adult-onset progressive ataxia from deletions/loss of function) and with Gillespie syndrome (ataxia with aniridia).
MRI commonly shows cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia, particularly of the vermis, but may be normal in early infancy.
A static course distinguishes it from progressive degenerative ataxias and should prompt genetic testing rather than a label of cerebral palsy.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA29 is caused by pathogenic variants in ITPR1, which encodes the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor type 1 (IP3R1), a large tetrameric intracellular calcium-release channel located on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and expressed at very high levels in cerebellar Purkinje cells. IP3R1 releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores in response to IP3 generated downstream of metabotropic glutamate receptor signalling, and this calcium flux is central to Purkinje cell dendritic function, synaptic plasticity (long-term depression) and cell survival. Missense variants, which often cluster in the IP3-binding or channel-forming domains, act through dominant-negative or loss-of-function mechanisms that disrupt calcium homeostasis and Purkinje cell signalling, producing the congenital non-progressive phenotype. By contrast, larger heterozygous deletions and haploinsufficiency of ITPR1 tend to cause the later-onset progressive SCA15 phenotype, while particular variant combinations with additional ocular features underlie Gillespie syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: SCA15 (ITPR1 loss of function) — allelic and later-onset
Other early-onset genetic ataxias (CACNA1A, CACNA1G, KCNC3, EBF3)
Joubert syndrome and related cerebellar malformations (molar tooth sign)
Cerebellar hypoplasia from perinatal injury or extreme prematurity
Congenital disorders of glycosylation with cerebellar involvement
additionalInvestigations: ITPR1 sequencing within an early-onset ataxia panel, with deletion/duplication analysis (MLPA or chromosomal microarray)
Brain MRI to assess the cerebellar vermis and exclude the molar tooth sign of Joubert syndrome
Ophthalmology review for nystagmus and to exclude the aniridia of Gillespie syndrome
Metabolic screen including transferrin isoform (glycosylation) studies to exclude mimics
Parental testing to determine de novo status and define recurrence risk
redFlags: Clear clinical or radiological progression, which should prompt reconsideration or a search for a second diagnosis
Aniridia or iris hypoplasia suggesting Gillespie syndrome
Molar tooth sign or episodic abnormal breathing suggesting Joubert syndrome
reference.prognosis: Usually static or very slowly progressive; most children eventually achieve independent walking, albeit delayed, and have a normal life expectancy. Ataxia and dysarthria persist and cognition is variably affected.
pitfalls: Labelling a static congenital ataxia as cerebral palsy and not pursuing genetic testing
Assuming autosomal dominant inheritance requires an affected parent when many cases are de novo
Missing the ITPR1 diagnosis by using expansion-only spinocerebellar ataxia panels
Overlooking aniridia that would reclassify the case as Gillespie syndrome
management: With no disease-modifying therapy, provide early developmental intervention and neurorehabilitation: physiotherapy for hypotonia and motor delay, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy
Arrange educational support and neuropsychological input for the learning difficulties and cognitive impairment seen in a subset
Obtain ophthalmology review for nystagmus and to exclude the aniridia of the allelic Gillespie syndrome
Institute falls prevention and provide mobility aids as the child achieves delayed independent walking
Offer genetic counselling with parental testing to determine de novo status and define recurrence risk, remembering many cases are de novo so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis
